lead: Software engineering is not a box of tools. It is a layered discipline: a quality focus at the base, a process above it, methods above that, and tools on top. Underneath sits a personal discipline called the essence of practice: understand the problem, plan a solution, carry out the plan, examine the result. General principles — simplicity, abstraction, modularity, separation of concerns, anticipating change — turn that discipline into decisions a team can defend. Teams use this structure on every sprint, and examiners test whether you can tell a tool from a process.
prereq: You need Chapter 1.1 for what software is and why different software types need different engineering effort.

sections.h3: Four layers: quality focus, process, methods, tools

blocks.text: Software engineering is drawn as a stack. The base is the quality focus: the team's commitment to a stated quality target, not just shipping code. Example: at most 2 defects per thousand lines of code (KLOC) at release. That number shapes later choices.

Above quality sits the process. A process is the framework of activities and their order: who plans, who reviews, when testing starts, what a phase or sprint must produce. A process is not a tool. It is the agreed way work moves.

Methods are the technical how: analysis techniques, design notations such as UML, review checklists, test-design techniques. Tools are software that supports process and methods: an IDE, Git, Jira, a CI server.
A tool with no process is a faster way to do the wrong thing. A process with no methods produces paperwork. The layers hold each other up.
Under every process model, each engineer repeats four moves. They look simple; skipping one is the most common cause of rework.

items: Understand the problem: name the user, what they must do, and what done means before writing code.
Plan the solution: sketch design, data, interfaces and work order; record assumptions.
Carry out the plan: build, test as you go, keep the plan visible and update it when facts change.
Examine the result: compare output with the original need, not with your own code; collect review and test evidence.

blocks.text: Each step leaves a small artifact: a note, a sketch, a test, a review record. Those artifacts make work repeatable when a teammate leaves. Practice is not only a phase at the start; it repeats at every scale, from a two-hour bug fix to a year-long release. Whatever the model (see 1.5), these four moves are the content.
Principles are short rules that survive changes of process model.

items: Keep it simple: fewer moving parts for the same need, not fewer lines.
Provide value: an unused feature is cost, not progress.
Build for maintainability: someone else will change this code.
Separate concerns: one module, one reason to change.
Modularity: parts that can be built and tested alone.
Abstraction: hide detail behind a clear interface.
Anticipate change: isolate rates, formats and vendors likely to move.
Build quality in: reviews and tests belong to construction.
Think before coding: ten minutes of design can save a day of debugging.

blocks.text: Principles sometimes conflict; simplicity and anticipating change pull opposite ways. Write down the trade-off you chose.

sections.h3: Practice areas, ethics, and the tool trap

blocks.text: Practice groups into five areas. Communication elicits requirements. Planning sets scope, estimates, schedule and risk (Unit 6). Modeling produces analysis and design sketches (Units 2 and 3). Construction writes code, unit-tests and integrates. Deployment delivers, configures and supports the running system.

Ethics belongs to practice. Shipping a known safety defect, hiding test failures, or copying code without a licence breaks the discipline even when the code runs. Public safety, honest results, privacy and licence respect are the lines.

Tools sit on top because they are easiest to buy and least decisive. A team that buys five tools but defines no process has added five things to maintain, not five improvements. Tools support a process; they never define one.

figure.caption: The worked example on the stack: 2 tools (Git, Jira) become 7 after buying 5 more, methods hold 1 review checklist, process holds 1 sprint, and the quality target allows 50 defects. The process layer is the one to watch: it stays at 1, so it remains the weak layer.

spec.aria: A stack with tools at the top showing 2 tools (Git, Jira) rising to 7, then 1 review checklist as methods, a highlighted 1 sprint process, and a quality-focus base allowing 50 defects.

examples.question: A six-person team runs two-week sprints, so one sprint is 10 working days. The product is 25 KLOC and the release target is at most 2 defects per KLOC. The team uses Git and Jira, one code-review checklist, and one sprint process. Map each item to a layer. Compute the maximum allowed defects at release. The manager then buys 5 more tools: how many tools now, and which layer is still weak if no process changes?
steps: One sprint = 2 weeks × 5 working days = 10 working days.
Quality target = 2 defects/KLOC × 25 KLOC = 50 defects allowed.
After buying 5 tools: 2 + 5 = 7 tools. Process stays at 1; no process change, so the process layer is weak.
examples.answer: Layers: tools 2, methods 1, process 1, quality focus 50 allowed defects; after the purchase there are 7 tools and the process layer remains the weak one.
examples.check:
kloc = 25
target = 2
tools = 2
methods = 1
process = 1
days = 2 * 5
allowed = target * kloc
new_tools = tools + 5
for v in (days, tools, methods, process, allowed, new_tools):
    print(v)

traps: Calling a toolchain the software process. Git and Jira support a process; they do not say who reviews, when testing starts, or what done means.
Putting tools at the base. The base is quality focus; tools are the top layer.
Treating understand the problem as requirement gathering only. It also means agreeing what done looks like and what the user must be able to do.
Listing simplicity as write the fewest lines. Simplicity is fewer moving parts for the same need, not code golf.
Mixing methods with process. A checklist or UML diagram is a method; the sequence of activities is the process.

quiz.q: Name the four layers of software engineering from base to top.
List the four steps of the essence of practice.
quiz.a: Understand the problem, plan the solution, carry out the plan, examine the result.

quiz.q: Why is a tool not a process?
quiz.a: A tool supports work; a process defines the activities, order and products. Git stores code but does not decide who reviews or when testing starts.

quiz.q: A 40 KLOC product has a quality target of 1.5 defects per KLOC. What is the maximum allowed defects?
A team has 3 tools, 2 methods and 1 process. It adds 4 tools and 1 method. Count each layer.
A team ships on time with 9 defects per KLOC against a target of 2. Which layers are suspect, and what evidence would you collect?
quiz.a: Quality focus is weak because the target is missed. Process is suspect: reviews and test gates. Methods are suspect: test design and checklists. Evidence: review records, defect density by module, test coverage, escaped defects.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry the layers show up in how teams are assessed: process maturity audits the process, platform teams own the tools, and defect escape rate sits at the quality base. Research on AI coding assistants asks whether tools can absorb method work; today humans still own understanding the problem and examining the result. Search next for process maturity, defect density, and separation of concerns in architecture.
